templates.name: Blank completion, phrase options (word + preposition, a/an + word)
Blank completion, contrast clue (including received view then finding)
Blank completion, cause or consequence clue
Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options

items.passage: Retail chains in the United States could increase profits by varying prices across neighborhoods, yet Stefano DellaVigna and Matthew Gentzkow found that most chains’ prices are largely ______ local conditions: a chain’s stores charge nearly identical prices regardless of whether their customers are wealthy or poor and whether competition is intense or weak.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Unresponsive to” means not changing in reaction to. The text says that a chain’s stores charge nearly the same prices whatever the income of their customers and however much competition they face, even though the chains could earn more by varying them. The prices, in other words, do not change with local conditions.

A.why_wrong: Prices “calibrated to” local conditions would be adjusted to fit each neighborhood, so they would differ from store to store. The text says the stores charge nearly the same prices.

B.why_wrong: “Inflated by” means pushed up by. The text never says that local conditions raise a chain’s prices; it says prices stay nearly the same whether customers are wealthy or poor.

D.why_wrong: Prices “tethered to” local conditions would be tied to them and so would move with them, which is the opposite of what DellaVigna and Gentzkow found.

sources.what: DellaVigna and Gentzkow, Uniform Pricing in US Retail Chains (NBER w23996; QJE 2019): most US food, drugstore and mass-merchandise chains charge nearly uniform prices across stores despite wide variation in consumer demographics and competition; the median chain sacrifices about $16m of annual profit; uniform pricing raises the prices poorer households pay relative to the rich

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (nearly the same prices whatever the customers or competition, although varying them would pay, so prices do not change with local conditions). Two reversals that tie prices to local conditions in different ways (fitted to, tied to) and one unsupported direction (pushed up by). Simplified: the paper also estimates the profit forgone and covers several kinds of chains; only the core finding is used. Raw freq.txt ranks: calibrated to 49,423; inflated by 22,778; unresponsive to 21,484; tethered to 17,743.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. Corrected option ranks 8,400 to 22,800 (3 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.22), one band; two steps (a concessive “could increase profits ... yet” plus a restating colon). Two reversals (calibrated to, tethered to) fall to the same stated fact, so not band 7.

items.passage: Much of composer Éliane Radigue’s electronic music evolves at a ______ pace, unfolding through a series of almost imperceptible tonal shifts: each of the three compositions in her Adnos cycle, which she created on an ARP 2500 synthesizer over eight years in the 1970s and 1980s, transforms over approximately 70 minutes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Glacial” here means extremely slow. The text says that Radigue’s music moves through tonal shifts so small they are almost imperceptible and that each Adnos piece takes roughly 70 minutes to transform, so the music changes very slowly.

B.why_wrong: “Frenetic” means wildly fast and excited. Shifts that are almost imperceptible and pieces that transform over 70 minutes describe music that changes slowly, not frantically.

C.why_wrong: “Staccato” is a musical term for short, sharply separated notes. The text describes the music as unfolding through tiny shifts, which suggests smooth, gradual change rather than abrupt, detached sounds.

D.why_wrong: “Erratic” means irregular and unpredictable. The text says nothing about sudden or irregular changes; it stresses how small and gradual the shifts are.

sources.what: Bandcamp Daily, Éliane Radigue’s Music Without End: her compositions ebb and flow through almost imperceptible tonal changes; the Adnos cycle, composed on the ARP 2500, three pieces created over eight years in the ’70s and ’80s, each slowly transforms over approximately 70 minutes

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (almost imperceptible shifts plus a 70-minute transformation, so the pace of change is very slow; key a familiar word in a transferred sense). Hedged to “much of” her music: the source says Adnos III is the most dynamic of the cycle. Raw freq.txt ranks: glacial 27,683; frenetic unseen; staccato 23,351; erratic 16,787. Reviewer: “ebbing and flowing” (the source’s own phrase, and a loose toehold for “erratic”, since ebb and flow can suggest an uneven pace) changed to “unfolding through a series of”.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. Options 9,500 (corrected; raw 27,700) to unseen, 3 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.64; key in a transferred sense (glacial = very slow). One-step restatement clue, so the difficulty is vocabulary and the figurative key.

fixes: passage: “ebbing and flowing through” changed to “unfolding through a series of” (removes a loose fit for “erratic” and the source’s own wording); why_wrong C updated

items.passage: Because subtle biases can operate without conscious awareness, one might expect them to be ______, persisting even once identified. Yet Devin Pope, Joseph Price, and Justin Wolfers found that after a study showing that NBA referees called more fouls against players of a different race attracted widespread media attention in 2007, the referees’ bias disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Intractable” means hard to change or get rid of. The blank describes what one might expect of biases that operate without conscious awareness: that they would persist even after being identified. “Yet” then introduces the contrasting finding that the referees’ bias disappeared once it was publicized.

A.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong side (ANT)
A.why_wrong: “Ephemeral” means short-lived. That describes what the researchers actually found, since the bias disappeared, not the expectation the blank describes, which “Yet” sets against the finding.

B.why_wrong: “Idiosyncratic” means peculiar to an individual. Nothing in the text concerns biases differing from person to person, and the word does not fit the restatement “persisting even once identified.”

C.why_wrong: “Willful” means deliberate and intentional. The text says these biases can operate without people’s awareness, so one would not expect them to be intentional.

sources.what: Pope, Price and Wolfers, Awareness Reduces Racial Bias (NBER w19765; Management Science 2018): bias in NBA referees’ foul calls persisted until widespread media attention in May 2007 following an academic study, then completely disappeared

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (the expectation is set up by a reason and a restatement, and “Yet” contrasts it with the finding; the finding’s own trait, ephemeral, is the trap). The expectation is framed as a reasoned guess (“one might expect”), not attributed to anyone. Simplified: the 2007 study was Price and Wolfers’s own; the bias was against players of the opposite race from the refereeing crew. Raw freq.txt ranks: ephemeral 21,660; idiosyncratic unseen; willful 21,615; intractable 38,422.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. All four options past 20,000 (mean log 4.81) and the band-7 B3 shape (blank on the expectation, the finding’s trait ephemeral as the trap), but the appositive “persisting even once identified” glosses the key, so it is one step for a student who knows intractable.

items.passage: In colonial India, agriculture depended on rainfall, and regional famines were commonplace. But as railroads reached more and more districts between 1861 and 1930, economists Robin Burgess and Dave Donaldson found, a rainfall shortfall in a district became less ______: local prices and mortality rates grew less responsive to it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Calamitous” means disastrous. Burgess and Donaldson found that once railroads reached a district, local prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall of rain. A drought that no longer drove up prices and deaths as much was less of a disaster for the people there.

A.recipe: wrong nuance: frequency instead of severity (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: “Recurrent” means happening again and again. Railroads could not change how often rain fell short; the text says only that prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall, which concerns how harmful it was, not how often it happened.

C.why_wrong: “Acrimonious” means bitter and angry, as a quarrel can be. The text says nothing about disputes over rainfall shortfalls.

D.why_wrong: “Quotidian” means ordinary or everyday. The text says nothing about shortfalls becoming more or less ordinary; it describes how much they affected prices and mortality rates.

band7_moves: negation hidden in a comparative (“became less ______”), as in d7807ec8 (“less ______ observers countered”)
near-synonym distractor that fails on one feature: recurrent (how often) against calamitous (how harmful)
all four options past rank 20,000; rarest distractor unseen in freq.txt
clue in the economists’ register (prices and death rates less responsive) one level more abstract than the key

sources.what: Burgess and Donaldson, Can Openness to Trade Reduce Income Volatility? Evidence from Colonial India’s Famine Era (LSE 2012): railroads expanding 1861 to 1930, rain-fed agriculture and commonplace regional famines; railroads made local prices less responsive to rainfall shocks, and mortality rates became significantly less responsive to rainfall shocks

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (prices and death rates less responsive to a shortfall, so a shortfall did less harm; reject the frequency reading). No negation-flip distractor (the band-7 B5 recipe). Simplified: the paper also reports real incomes becoming less responsive; only prices and mortality are used. Raw freq.txt ranks: recurrent 23,668; calamitous 40,225; acrimonious 43,432; quotidian unseen.

band7.why: All four options past corrected 20,000 (calamitous 40,225; rarest distractor quotidian unseen; mean log 4.90), key not the rarest (band-5 guard clear). Negation hidden in the comparative “less ______” (band-7 B5 recipe, as d7807ec8), two steps (less responsive prices and deaths, so less harm), and recurrent and quotidian are built from the earlier “famines were commonplace” (frequency, not severity), as inconspicuousness is in 6017ae31. None fits: railroads cannot change how often rain fails.

items.passage:
The following text is from Harold Frederic’s 1896 novel The Damnation of Theron Ware. Theron has abruptly informed his wife, Alice, that he must depart tonight.

Alice’s face showed surprise, but no trace of suspicion. She spoke with <u>studied</u> amiability during the meal, and deferred with such unexpected tact to his implied desire not to be questioned as to the mysterious motives of the journey, that his mood instinctively softened and warmed toward her, as they finished supper.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “studied” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “studied” describes Alice’s amiability as something she produces on purpose. She is surprised by Theron’s sudden journey yet shows no suspicion, and she defers “with such unexpected tact” to his wish not to be questioned: her friendliness is a careful, intentional effort, so “studied” most nearly means deliberate.

A.why_wrong: To study something can mean to scrutinize it, or examine it closely, but Alice is not examining anything; “studied” describes the kind of amiability she shows.

B.why_wrong: A studied person can be learned, or scholarly, but nothing in the text concerns learning; the word describes the care Alice takes in being friendly.

D.why_wrong: The text says Alice’s face showed “no trace of suspicion,” so her amiability is not distrustful; she defers to Theron with “unexpected tact,” and his mood warms toward her.

sources.what: Text of The Damnation of Theron Ware (Harold Frederic, 1896), copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. Excerpt copied exactly (one paragraph); the intro summarizes Theron’s speech just before it (“I find I must go to Albany tonight”). Target studied is an everyday word in its adjectival sense (done with deliberate effort). Steps: 2 (set aside the everyday sense; read the surprise and the unexpected tact as signs of effort). Written as band 6: the M1 band-6 model 9b22bf7b keys Dictate against senses of determine. Raw freq.txt ranks: Scrutinized 18,297; Scholarly 5,349; Deliberate 4,546; Distrustful 23,256. Reviewer: hardened from Examined, Academic, Reluctant (mean log rank 3.57, under the band-6 M1 model 9b22bf7b at 3.67 and the band-7 M1 models at 3.84 to 3.88; two distractors made no sense in the sentence and Reluctant could be read loosely as “forced”). Now two rarer senses of study (scrutinize, learned) and a topic echo of “suspicion” that the text rules out; all four options between ranks 4,500 and 23,000, mean log 4.00. Senses that would be a second answer (premeditated, calculated, contrived, affected, feigned, rehearsed) kept out.

band7.why: Was nearer band 5: two distractors (Examined, Academic) made no sense in the sentence and the set sat at mean log 3.57. After the fix all four options sit at 4,500 to 23,000 (mean log 4.00, above the band-6 and band-7 M1 models), the target is a secondary sense of an everyday word, and two distractors are real senses of study. No band-7 claim: M1 band 7 relies on senses that fit loosely, which this item avoids by design.

fixes: hardened: options Examined, Academic, Reluctant replaced by Scrutinized, Scholarly, Distrustful (mean log rank 3.57 to 4.00, one frequency band; Reluctant could be read loosely as forced); why_wrong rewritten

items.passage: A snowshoe hare whose coat has turned white for winter is hardly ______ on brown, snowless ground. Tracking radio-collared hares in Montana, Marketa Zimova and colleagues found that hares whose coats did not match their surroundings were noticeable to predators and experienced lower weekly survival.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Camouflaged” means hidden by blending in with the surroundings. The text says that hares whose coats did not match their surroundings were noticeable to predators, so a white hare on snowless ground is hardly blending in: it is easy to spot.

B.why_wrong: Saying the hare is “hardly vulnerable” would mean it is safe, but the text says mismatched hares were noticeable to predators and had lower weekly survival.

C.why_wrong: “Nocturnal” means active at night. The text is about whether a hare’s coat matches the ground, not about when hares are active.

D.why_wrong: “Sluggish” means slow-moving. The text says nothing about how fast the hares move; it is about how visible they are.

sources.what: NC State Southeast Climate Adaptation Science Center, Evolutionary clock ticks for snowshoe hares facing climate change: radio-collared snowshoe hares in Montana; white hares stand out to predators against snowless backgrounds; mismatched hares’ weekly survival decreases (Zimova et al., Ecology Letters)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key letter A. The key camouflaged is unseen in freq.txt only because that corpus is 1850 to 1928 prose; it is a common modern word, so the set is not the band-5 pattern (rare key, common distractors). Negated frame “hardly ______”; one negation flip (vulnerable), one topic echo, one unsupported word. Simplified: the weekly survival figures (about 96 to 89 percent) are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: camouflaged unseen; vulnerable 23,199; nocturnal 19,332; sluggish 11,947.

items.passage: The bioluminescence of New Zealand glowworm larvae (Arachnocampa luminosa) is ______ their feeding strategy. Each larva constructs a silk nest on a cave ceiling and suspends as many as 30 silk threads studded with adhesive droplets; its light then attracts small flying insects, particularly midges, into those sticky filaments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Integral to” means essential to. The text explains that a glowworm larva catches food with sticky threads and that its light is what draws flies into them, so the glow is an essential part of how the larvae feed.

A.why_wrong: “Incidental to” means a minor side feature of. The light is what draws prey into the threads, so it is central to feeding, not incidental.

B.why_wrong: “Detrimental to” means harmful to. The glow helps the larvae feed by luring flies into their threads; nothing suggests it hinders feeding.

C.why_wrong: “Reminiscent of” means calling to mind. The glow is part of the larvae’s way of feeding, not something that brings it to mind.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Arachnocampa luminosa: endemic to New Zealand; the larva spins a silk nest on the cave ceiling and hangs down up to 30 silk threads with small sticky droplets; the glow acts as bait, attracting prey (largely small Diptera, especially midges) into the threads

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Key letter D. Restatement over a semicolon (the light draws flies into the feeding threads). All four options adjective plus preposition. Raw freq.txt ranks: incidental to 19,860; detrimental to 28,955; reminiscent of 20,349; integral to 30,924.

items.passage: Analyzing vocabulary from 2,474 languages, Joshua Conrad Jackson and colleagues found that all language families categorize emotions primarily by how pleasant and how physiologically arousing they are, yet emotion concepts are also ______ cultures: Nakh-Dagestanian languages associate “grief” with “fear” and “anxiety,” whereas Tai-Kadai languages associate it with “regret.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Divergent across” means differing from one to another. After noting what all language families share, the text turns with “yet” to differences: grief is linked with fear and anxiety in one family of languages but with regret in another. Emotion concepts therefore differ across cultures.

A.why_wrong: If emotion concepts were indistinguishable across cultures, “grief” would be grouped with the same emotions everywhere, but the text gives an example in which it is not.

C.why_wrong: Concepts “insulated from” culture would be shielded from its influence. The example shows the meaning of “grief” differing between language families, so these concepts are not shielded from cultural differences.

D.why_wrong: “Subordinate to” means ranked below. The text does not compare the importance of emotion concepts and cultures; it shows that the concepts differ from one group of languages to another.

sources.what: UNC-Chapel Hill news release on Jackson et al., Science 2019: lead author Joshua Conrad Jackson; data from nearly 2,500 languages; all languages distinguish emotions primarily by whether they are pleasant or unpleasant and by low or high arousal; some languages view grief as similar to fear and anxiety, others as similar to regret

Neuroscience News (University of Otago release) for the details: 2,474 languages; hedonic valence and physiological activation; Nakh-Dagestanian languages link grief with fear and anxiety, Tai-Kadai languages with regret

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics). Key letter B. Contrast after “yet” plus an example. Lead author Joshua Conrad Jackson (Science 2019, with Joseph Watts and others); reviewer changed the credit from “Joseph Watts and colleagues”. Simplified: colexification (one word for several concepts) is described as how a language groups concepts. Raw freq.txt ranks: indistinguishable across 20,439; divergent across 35,999; insulated from 48,468; subordinate to 13,590.

fixes: credit changed from “Joseph Watts and colleagues” to “Joshua Conrad Jackson and colleagues” (lead author, Science 2019); UNC release naming Jackson added as first source

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: On September 8, 1965, Larry Itliong and more than 1,000 Filipino farmworkers walked off vineyards in Delano, California. Growers responded by hiring Mexican farmworkers to cross the picket lines. To ______ this tactic, Itliong asked César Chávez to bring his largely Mexican farmworkers’ association into the strike, and its supporters voted overwhelmingly to join.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Thwart” means to prevent from succeeding. Growers were using Mexican farmworkers to break the Filipino workers’ strike. By bringing a largely Mexican farmworkers’ association into the strike, Itliong aimed to keep that tactic from working.

A.why_wrong: To “emulate” a tactic is to copy it. Itliong did not hire replacement workers; he sought allies to strengthen the strike.

B.why_wrong: To “publicize” a tactic is to make it widely known. The text describes Itliong recruiting another union, not drawing public attention to what the growers did.

D.why_wrong: To “condone” a tactic is to accept it. Asking a largely Mexican union to join the strike worked against the growers’ use of Mexican strikebreakers.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Delano grape strike: on September 8, 1965, Itliong and more than 1,000 Filipino farm workers walked off vineyards; growers hired Mexican farm workers to cross the picket lines and break the strike; Itliong sought out Cesar Chavez, leader of the predominantly Mexican NFWA, to keep the strike from failing; NFWA supporters voted overwhelmingly to join

items.notes: Subject: history (US labor). Key letter C. Purpose clause “To ______ this tactic” with the cause in the sentence before. Simplified: AWOC and NFWA are not named; the NFWA is described as the source does (predominantly Mexican). Raw freq.txt ranks: emulate 26,669; publicize unseen; thwart 11,137; condone 20,883.

items.passage:
The following text is from Henryk Sienkiewicz’s 1891 novel Without Dogma (translated by Iza Young in 1893). The narrator’s guest Kromitzki has delivered a lengthy monologue about his commercial affairs.

[Kromitzki] did not cease talking, but went on <u>in the same strain</u> while with the help of the servant he unpacked his portmanteau. Sometimes he interrupted his flow of words in order to show me some specimens brought from the East.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “in the same strain” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Kromitzki has been talking at length about his business, and the text says he “did not cease talking” and kept up his “flow of words” while unpacking. He went on talking as he had been, so “in the same strain” most nearly means in the same manner.

B.why_wrong: A strain can be a great effort, but the text is about Kromitzki continuing to talk as before, not about how hard he was working.

C.why_wrong: A strain can be stress or pressure, but nothing in the text suggests Kromitzki was under pressure; he simply kept talking.

D.why_wrong: A strain can be an injury to a muscle, but nothing in the text mentions an injury; the phrase describes how he went on talking.

sources.what: Text of Without Dogma (Henryk Sienkiewicz, 1891; translated from the Polish by Iza Young, 1893), copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter A. Excerpt copied exactly from one paragraph, trimmed at sentence ends (the opening sentence, in which the narrator shows Kromitzki to his room after tea, and the closing sentence, which ends in a colon, are dropped; “[Kromitzki]” replaces “He”). The intro summarizes the paragraph before it (“a long-winded harangue about his affairs”). All three distractors are other senses of strain (effort, stress, muscle injury). Raw freq.txt ranks: In the same manner 387; With equal exertion 7,464; Under the same pressure 3,093; With the same injury 4,796.

items.passage: After earning a doctorate in zoology in 1907, Charles Henry Turner struggled to obtain an academic position and spent most of his career teaching at Sumner High School in St. Louis. He was nonetheless a ______ researcher, continuing to conduct and publish studies of insect behavior throughout his career.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Persistent” means continuing steadily despite difficulty. Although Turner could not find an academic job and taught high school instead, he kept carrying out and publishing research on insects throughout his career.

A.why_wrong: A reluctant researcher would be unwilling to do research, but Turner kept doing it throughout his career despite his difficulties.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that Turner was reckless in his research.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about Turner being cautious; it stresses that he kept researching and publishing despite obstacles.

sources.what: US-RSE Black History Month spotlight, Charles Henry Turner: PhD in zoology 1907; faced problems finding a job in academia; spent most of his career at Sumner High School in St. Louis; continued to pursue his research and publication throughout his career (bee color vision, insect hearing)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (history of zoology). Key letter B. Clue: “nonetheless” plus the participial restatement. The publication count (about 70 papers) is left out: the reachable source does not state it. Raw freq.txt ranks: reluctant 6,398; persistent 6,336; reckless 3,186; cautious 5,680.

items.passage: Artist Do Ho Suh’s replicas of residences he has inhabited, including his childhood home in Seoul and his New York apartment, are surprisingly ______. Each is constructed from translucent silk or polyester fabric, so within a few hours an entire house can be folded up and packed into a suitcase.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Portable” means easy to carry. The text explains that each replica is made of thin sheets of fabric, so an entire house can be folded and packed into a suitcase.

A.why_wrong: Works that can be folded up and packed away within hours are the opposite of fixed or permanent structures.

B.why_wrong: “Ornate” means elaborately decorated. The text describes the replicas’ material and how they pack, not any decoration.

C.why_wrong: “Cluttered” means crowded with things. Nothing in the text describes the replicas as full of objects.

sources.what: Tatler Asia on Do Ho Suh: childhood home recreated in Korean silk organza, New York apartment in translucent polyester; in a matter of hours one person could fold up all the rooms and squeeze the entire house into a suitcase

items.notes: Subject: humanities (art). Key letter D. Blank in the first sentence, restated by the second (folded and packed into a suitcase). Raw freq.txt ranks: permanent 6,682; ornate 21,070; cluttered 44,609; portable 20,596.

items.passage: White-throated sparrows in Canada traditionally concluded their song with three notes. A two-note variation emerged in British Columbia by the 1990s and spread eastward, and by 2015 it had ______ the original ending west of central Ontario, where every sparrow was singing the new version.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Displaced” means taken the place of. By 2015 every sparrow west of central Ontario was singing the new two-note version, so it had taken the place of the traditional three-note ending there.

A.why_wrong: The new version did not copy the old ending; it ended with two notes instead of three, and by 2015 every sparrow in the region sang it instead.

B.why_wrong: To precede something is to come before it. The three-note ending was the traditional one, so the two-note version came after it, not before.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that the new version protected the old ending; by 2015 no sparrow in the region was still singing it.

sources.what: National Geographic on Otter et al. 2020 (Current Biology): the old song ends in a triplet, the new one in a two-tone couplet; it emerged by the 1990s in northern British Columbia and spread east; by 2015 every sparrow west of central Ontario was singing the doublet ending

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal behavior). Key letter C. Context first, blank last; the clause after it restates. Raw freq.txt ranks: copied 10,080; preceded 7,223; displaced 18,095; protected 2,995.

items.passage: The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona can ______ the sonar that big brown bats use to hunt. Aaron Corcoran and colleagues found that the moth’s ultrasonic clicks jam the bats’ echolocation: the bats frequently tried to capture clicking moths but had great difficulty doing so.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Disrupt” means to interfere with. The text says the moth’s clicks jam the bats’ echolocation, so bats struggle to catch clicking moths: the moth interferes with the sonar bats use to hunt.

B.why_wrong: To boost the bats’ sonar would be to strengthen it, which would help the bats. The moth’s clicks jam the sonar instead.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the moth moving faster than the bats’ sonar; it says the moth’s clicks interfere with that sonar.

D.why_wrong: To intensify the sonar would be to make it stronger. The moth’s clicks make the sonar less effective, not more.

sources.what: Mongabay on Corcoran, Barber and Conner 2009 (Science): the tiger moth Bertholdia trigona eludes big brown bats by jamming their echolocation with ultrasonic clicks; bats frequently tried to capture the clicking moths but had much difficulty

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology). Key letter A. Restatement after a sentence break and a colon (jam, great difficulty capturing). Raw freq.txt ranks: disrupt 66,226; boost 39,469; outpace unseen; intensify 24,149.

items.passage:
The following text is from Stephen Leacock’s 1912 book Sunshine Sketches of a Little Town. Billy, a clerk at Mr. Smith’s hotel, delivers a telegram.

“Here’s your wire, sir,” he said.

“What does it say?” said Mr. Smith.

He always dealt with written documents with a fine <u>air</u> of detachment. I don’t suppose there were ten people in Mariposa who knew that Mr. Smith couldn’t read.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “air” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Mr. Smith, who cannot read, asks the clerk what the telegram says as though he could not be bothered to look. The narrator says he dealt with documents with “a fine air of detachment”: an outward manner of not caring that hides the fact that he cannot read. “Air” most nearly means manner.

A.why_wrong: Air can mean moving air, as in a breeze, but here the word describes how Mr. Smith appears when he handles documents.

C.why_wrong: An air can be a tune, but nothing in the text involves music; the word describes Mr. Smith’s behavior.

D.why_wrong: “The air” can mean the sky or the heavens, but the text is about the way Mr. Smith deals with written documents, not about anything overhead.

sources.what: Text of Sunshine Sketches of a Little Town (Stephen Leacock, 1912), copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter B. Excerpt copied exactly from three consecutive paragraphs (straight quotes and apostrophes made curly). All three distractors are other senses of air. Raw freq.txt ranks: Breeze 2,421; Manner 387; Melody 5,826; Heavens 676.

items.passage:
The following text is from Grace King’s 1893 short story “A Delicate Affair.” Madame, who is approaching eighty, is playing solitaire.

Mr. Horace was as old as she, but he looked much younger, although his dress and appearance <u>betrayed</u> no evidence of an effort in that direction. Whenever his friend cheated, he would invariably call her attention to it; and as usual she would shrug her shoulders, and say, “Bah! lose a game for a card!” and pursue the conversation.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “betrayed” most nearly mean?

The following text is from John Galsworthy’s 1906 novel The Man of Property. Old Jolyon has been conversing late into the night with his son, young Jolyon.

The clock <u>struck</u> one before old Jolyon had finished, and at the sound of its striking his principles came back. He took out his watch with a look of surprise:

“I must go to bed, Jo,” he said.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “struck” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The text refers to “the sound of its striking,” and old Jolyon then checks his watch and says he must go to bed. The clock sounded the hour of one, so “struck” most nearly means chimed.

A.why_wrong: To strike can mean to find something, as in striking gold, but a clock does not unearth anything; it marks the hour with a sound.

B.why_wrong: To strike can mean to hit or attack, but the clock is not attacking anyone; the text mentions the sound it makes.

D.why_wrong: To be struck by something can mean to be dazzled or impressed by it, but here the clock is marking the time, not affecting anyone’s feelings.

items.passage: Elizabeth Cotten’s distinctive guitar technique was ______ her left-handedness. Self-taught, she played a guitar strung for right-handed musicians upside down, so she plucked the bass lines with her fingers and the melody with her thumb, an approach that became known as “Cotten picking.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A product of” means a result of. Because she was left-handed, Cotten turned a right-handed guitar upside down, and that is why she played the bass with her fingers and the melody with her thumb. Her style resulted from her left-handedness.

A.why_wrong: Her style did not take the place of her left-handedness; it came about because of it.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests her style endangered her left-handedness; the text says the style grew out of the way a left-handed player held a right-handed guitar.

D.why_wrong: A reward is given in return for something. Her style was not given to her in return for being left-handed; it resulted from the way she had to hold the guitar.

items.passage: Volunteers in a study led by Ting Zhang placed everyday material, such as songs they were listening to, into time capsules early one summer and predicted how curious they would be to open them. At summer’s end, their predictions ______ their actual curiosity: they were considerably more curious than they had anticipated.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

B.why_wrong: Predictions that went beyond the volunteers’ curiosity would mean they were less curious than expected, which is the reverse of the finding the text points to.

C.why_wrong: Predictions that kept pace with their curiosity would have been accurate, but the volunteers turned out to be more curious than they had predicted.

D.why_wrong: To make up for something is to compensate for it. Predictions cannot compensate for curiosity; the text compares how curious the volunteers expected to be with how curious they were.
